lesson.title: Compound Noun Engineering
lesson.subtitle: Handschuh = hand-shoe. German builds words like Lego — and English does too.

hook.title: The Lego Grammar
hook.content: German has a reputation for impossible long words. It has actually just refused to forget how English words used to be built. Handschuh is hand-shoe (a glove). Zahnarzt is tooth-doctor (a dentist). Krankenhaus is sick-people-house (a hospital). English once built exactly the same way — and still does, half asleep: cup-board became cupboard, break-fast became breakfast. The difference: German writes its Lego without dropping pieces. When you meet a German monster word, you do not translate it. You take it apart.

footnotes.title: The Head Word Wears the Pants
footnotes.content: The LAST piece of a compound runs the show — its gender, its plural, its meaning core. das Haus → das Krankenhaus (neuter). der Zug → der Aufzug (masculine). Learn the last piece and you own the whole word.

pattern.title: Split, Read, Predict
pattern.content: Splitting: Handschuh = Hand + Schuh. Feuerzeug = Feuer + Zeug ('fire-stuff' — a lighter). Fernseher = fern + Seher ('far-seer' — a television). Staubsauger = Staub + Sauger ('dust-sucker' — a vacuum cleaner). Reading rule: split at the last plausible noun, then ask what a 'X-Y' would literally be. Gender rule: der Apfel + der Kuchen = der Apfelkuchen — the head (Kuchen) donates the article. Your own vocabulary compounds for free: Haus + Tür? Tür is taught — Haustür, the front door, literally house-door.
pattern.trap_note: Your mind will offer: “a compound's gender is a new thing to learn.” It is not. The LAST word is the head and it donates its gender to the whole compound: das Krankenhaus, because Haus is das. Never memorise a compound's article — read the tail.
pattern.linguist_note: English and German both inherited compounding from Proto-Germanic; English then wore its compounds smooth (lord ← hlāf-weard, 'loaf-ward' — the bread-keeper!). German's transparent writing system is the conservative option, not the strange one.

exercises.prompt: Compound gender rule: der Apfel + der Kuchen = ?
options: der Apfelkuchen — the last noun donates the gender
exercises.target_answer: der Apfelkuchen — the last noun donates the gender
exercises.explanation: The final piece is the grammatical head: its article, its plural, its meaning core. das Haus → das Krankenhaus.

exercises.prompt: Split it: 'Handschuh' is literally 'hand-shoe' — what is the real word in English?
exercises.explanation: German describes the function; English kept a Norse word. Both languages agree a glove is footwear for your hand. And when the compound cake schmeckt — taste ↔ schmecken, smack's cousin — the compound rule still holds: der Kuchen donates the gender.

exercises.prompt: Match each transparent compound with its literal reading:
exercises.target_answer: der Zahnarzt, das Feuerzeug, der Staubsauger, der Fernseher, die Hauptstadt
exercises.meaning: dentist, lighter, vacuum cleaner, television, capital (city)
exercises.explanation: German calqued the Greek/Latin science words from native parts — read the parts and the meaning is free. The head word donates the gender: Arzt → der, Stadt → die.

exercises.prompt: Build the dentist from Lego parts (tooth + doctor):
exercises.explanation: Zahn + Arzt = Zahnarzt. Same factory: Augenarzt (eye-doctor), Tierarzt (animal-doctor). And the compound feelings ride the same shelf: der Mut (mood's twin), der Wunsch, das Glück — luck, the one English borrowed back.

exercises.idea: you're introducing your neighbors to a friend: the man and the woman have a child
cues: Flags first: der Mann, die Frau — then the plural verb joins them: haben ein Kind
exercises.target_answer: Der Mann und die Frau haben ein Kind
exercises.meaning: The man and the woman have a child
exercises.explanation: Two subjects, plural verb, ein Kind — the family trio with their flags: der, die, das.

summary.outcome: Split compounds, read them literally, and predict gender from the head noun.

use_example.german: Der Mann und die Frau haben ein Kind.
use_example.english: The man and the woman have a child.

summary.takeaway: Compounds are Lego: split at the last noun, read literally, and let the head word donate the gender.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the 32 Calques Deep-Dive — the curated compound gallery from Kühlschrank to Backpfeife.

twist.prompt: Hearing check — negate the noun: they have a child becomes they have NO child. (kein, declined like ein.)
twist.explanation: Kind is neuter, so kein stays bare: kein Kind. nicht is for verbs — the noun loses its 'one' instead. And the plural verb tells you Sie is 'they', not the formal 'you'.

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

wort.etymology_derivation: Final d → t. Plural: Wörter / Worte.

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

mann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mann- — the identical twin of man; German keeps the short a English lengthened. [wiktionary]

frau.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ 'lady, mistress' — kin to archaic English frow 'lady'; Fräulein andMs.-style Frauennamen carry the same root. [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

zahnarzt.context_translation: The dentist looks at my teeth.
zahnarzt.etymology_derivation: Zahn (tooth) + Arzt (doctor) - literally tooth-doctor; Zahn shows the t-to-z shift from the same ancient root as English tooth (PIE *h₃dónts). [wiktionary]

hauptstadt.context_phrase: Berlin ist die Hauptstadt von Deutschland.
hauptstadt.context_translation: Berlin is the capital of Germany.
hauptstadt.etymology_derivation: Haupt + Stadt, literally head city; the page traces Haupt to the PIE head root that also yields Latin caput, so English capital is the Latin twin, and Stadt is the twin of English stead. [wiktionary]

glück.etymology_derivation: Probably borrowed from Old Dutch *gilukki — Wiktionary: 'Compare English luck' (a relative via Dutch). [wiktionary]

mut.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *modaz — the page lists English mood as the cognate: the English d became German t (day and Tag), and courage is having the right mood. [wiktionary]

wunsch.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wunska — the page lists English wish among the cognates; the verb is wünschen. [wiktionary]

schmecken.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *smakkijan — Wiktionary: 'Compare English smack and smatch'. [wiktionary]

witwe.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *widuwǭ, Old High German wituwa, the twin of English widow, which comes from Old English widuwe. [wiktionary]

raum.context_phrase: Der Raum ist groß und hell.
raum.context_translation: The room is large and bright.
raum.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *rūmą (space); the same word as English room — German diphthongized the long u to au. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
